items.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut large language model prices by up to 80% over several months amid competitive pressure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
items.summary:
OpenAI and Anthropic have significantly reduced the prices of their large language models (LLMs) since June 2026, with cuts reaching up to 80%. These reductions include OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Luna and Sol models and Anthropic's Claude series, reflecting a rapid decrease in cost without apparent compromises in output quality. The price cuts appear to be a response to competitive dynamics between the two companies, aiming to make LLM usage more affordable for various applications, including agentic coding.

The timeline of announcements shows a pattern of tit-for-tat price adjustments, with both companies lowering input, output, and cache read token costs. Notably, cache read costs, which dominate token expenditure in agent-based coding, have been reduced by up to 75%, significantly lowering overall usage costs. Despite the price drops, model performance has generally remained stable or improved, with newer versions like Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol offering competitive benchmarks.

These price reductions have contributed to a broader trend of decreasing cost-per-token in the LLM market, even as aggregate spending rises due to increased adoption and improved model capabilities. The moves highlight the evolving economics of AI services and the strategic pricing responses by leading AI providers to maintain market share and encourage wider usage.

items.title: Analysis: AI panic mirrors early capitalism fears through a 'cognitive mercantilism' lens, equating intelligence to scarce wealth and control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cognitive Mercantilism: AI panic resembles fears of early capitalism
items.summary:
The article draws parallels between contemporary AI anxiety and the mercantilist worldview preceding capitalism, framing AI panic as a form of 'cognitive mercantilism.' It argues that just as early capitalism emerged by shifting from a zero-sum view of wealth to recognizing wealth creation, current fears treat intelligence as a fixed, scarce resource to be hoarded and controlled.

It outlines four key beliefs of mercantilism—scarcity of wealth, distrust of ordinary people, focus on supply control, and limited roles for most people—and shows how these map onto current attitudes toward intelligence and AI. Intelligence is seen as a resource to be accumulated and guarded by elites, with ordinary people viewed as limited consumers rather than active participants in knowledge creation.

The piece suggests this mindset shapes national and corporate strategies around talent and intellectual property, influencing regulation and societal views on democratizing intelligence. It highlights the risk of replicating outdated assumptions about scarcity and control in the cognitive domain amid AI's rise.

items.title: IBM CEO says open weight AI models now deliver 90% of frontier model performance at 10% of the cost for on-prem enterprise use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: IBM CEO says open weight models are now good and cheap on-prem
items.summary:
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna stated on the company's Q3 earnings call that open weight AI models have become highly cost-effective and nearly as capable as closed frontier models for on-premises enterprise applications. He highlighted that these models offer 90% of the performance at just 10% of the token cost, making them attractive for most business tasks such as email summarization and contract examination.

Krishna noted that while some tasks may still require the highest-performing models, the majority of enterprise AI needs can be met with these cheaper alternatives. He also mentioned growing interest in on-prem AI infrastructure, with IBM planning to provide software to simplify AI deployments and anticipating increased sales of its Spyre mainframe accelerator cards. IBM's infrastructure revenue grew modestly, while software and Red Hat products showed stronger growth in the quarter.

items.title: Researchers propose attention-free Grassmann flow architecture for sequence modeling, achieving competitive results with fewer parameters than Transformers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Attention Is Not What You Need (2025)
items.summary:
Researchers revisit the necessity of explicit self-attention in sequence modeling and introduce a novel attention-free architecture based on Grassmann flows. Their Causal Grassmann layer encodes local token pairs as two-dimensional subspaces on a Grassmann manifold, enabling information propagation through controlled deformations of low-rank subspaces rather than unstructured tensor spaces. This approach achieves validation perplexities within 10 to 15 percent of size-matched Transformers on the Wikitext-2 benchmark and slightly outperforms Transformer heads on the SNLI natural language inference task when combined with DistilBERT.

The study analyzes the complexity of Grassmann mixing, demonstrating linear scaling with sequence length for fixed rank, and suggests that manifold-based designs offer a more structured path toward geometric and invariant-based interpretations of neural reasoning. This work challenges the conventional reliance on multi-head attention mechanisms and proposes an alternative that may provide clearer mathematical interpretability in neural sequence models.

items.title: Researchers propose DIVA method for LLMs to optimize information seeking by valuing evidence based on decision impact and cost, reducing unnecessary checks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Not All Information Is Worth Asking For: Decision-Informed Information Seeking with LLMs
items.summary: Researchers introduce Decision-Informed Value-of-information Acquisition (DIVA), a training-free procedure that enables large language models (LLMs) to decide which evidence to seek and when to stop by modeling how each check affects decision outcomes and weighing its cost. DIVA lets LLMs specify a simple decision model through numeric inputs and evaluates candidate checks by their expected improvement to decisions, stopping when no further checks are cost-effective. Its variant, DIVA-U, accounts for uncertainty in these estimates. Across four domains and 20 LLMs, DIVA-U outperforms baselines by reducing decision regret, mainly by avoiding unnecessary evidence gathering, and DIVA cuts regret by 75% in synthetic scenarios with known check reliability. The approach applies broadly to any LLM without additional training, and code is publicly available.

Its variant, DIVA-U, accounts for uncertainty in these estimates. Across four domains and 20 LLMs, DIVA-U outperforms baselines by reducing decision regret, mainly by avoiding unnecessary evidence gathering, and DIVA cuts regret by 75% in synthetic scenarios with known check reliability. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support decisions under incomplete information, where deciding what to look up and when to stop matters as much as the final answer. However, LLMs fall into an information trap: They pay for checks, i.e., costly pieces of evidence, that cannot change their decision or are not worth their cost, and they keep asking when the evidence is already sufficient. To this end, we propose Decision-Informed Value-of-information Acquisition (DIVA), a simple yet effective procedure for LLM information seeking based on the decision value of evidence. DIVA 1) lets the LLM specify a small decision model, i.e., how likely a bad outcome is and how each check would shift this probability, through short numeric questions and 2) values each candidate check by how much its imagined outcomes improve the decision net of its cost, stopping when no check is worth its cost. Its variant, DIVA-U, further accounts for the LLM's uncertain estimates of how strongly each check shifts this probability. DIVA is training-free and applies to any LLM. Across four domains and 20 LLMs, DIVA-U has lower regret, i.e., value lost relative to the best possible decision, than every LLM baseline on real-world data, mainly by stopping once evidence suffices, and DIVA cuts the regret of the best LLM baseline by 75% in synthetic scenarios where every check's reliability is given. Code: github.com/seunghan96/diva.

items.title: Researchers introduce SWE-Shift benchmark to evaluate coding agents under mid-execution changes in software development, revealing performance drops across 17 systems including GPT-6 Astra [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SWE-Shift: Evaluating Coding Agents in Evolving Workspaces
items.summary: Researchers have developed SWE-Shift, a benchmark designed to assess coding agents' ability to handle evolving workspaces where code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements change during task execution. The benchmark includes 120 scenarios across 12 change families, testing agents on both uninterrupted (Clean) and updated (Shifted) task continuations. Evaluation of 17 coding-agent systems showed universally lower success rates on Shifted tasks compared to Clean ones, with GPT-6 Astra's success rate dropping from 67.35% to 24.79%. Tool and session changes, as well as stale evidence, resulted in zero paired success across all systems, highlighting challenges in preserving work and adapting to updates. These findings indicate that while agents may complete unchanged tasks successfully, they often fail to maintain valid work or recover state after mid-execution changes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Repository-level coding benchmarks largely assume that tasks and environments remain unchanged throughout execution. In software development, code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements can change while an agent is still working. We introduce SWE-Shift, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under such mid-execution changes. From the same saved history and workspace, a Clean continuation proceeds without intervention, while a matched Shifted continuation receives a task-relevant update. Success requires completing the current task, preserving still-valid work, and satisfying the applicable state and evidence checks. The benchmark contains 120 scenarios across 12 change families, each evaluated at nine scheduled intervention positions. We evaluate 17 coding-agent systems, all of which have lower Shifted than Clean success. GPT-6 Astra drops from 67.35% to 24.79%, with 20.34% paired success. Tool/session changes and stale evidence yield zero paired success across all systems. Late-position paired success is lower for some systems and higher for others. These results show that success on the unchanged task can coexist with failures to preserve work, recover state, or refresh evidence after an update.

items.title: DMAIC-Bench evaluates self-restraint in LLM agents across 97 multi-stage analytical tasks in industrial and life-science workflows, revealing challenges in evidence-based decision routing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DMAIC-Bench: From Self-Reflection to Self-Restraint for Agents in Multi-Stage Analytical Tasks
items.summary:
DMAIC-Bench introduces a benchmark to assess large language model (LLM) agents' ability to use intermediate evidence to decide whether to continue, redirect, or stop in multi-stage analytical tasks, a capability termed self-restraint. The benchmark includes 97 seeded tasks from 15 industrial cases across four sectors, using Lean Six Sigma's statistical criteria, and extends to 16 life-science tasks in RNA sequencing and genome-wide association studies. It uses paired counterfactual tasks to distinguish warranted restraint from indiscriminate stopping and evaluates agent execution traces with a private scorer and expert review.

Testing 13 models from six providers, DMAIC-Bench found high accuracy (92%) on decisions to proceed (GO) but low accuracy (19%) on decisions to stop (NO-GO), with many agents performing forbidden analyses despite correct diagnostics. Expert review of 11 audited agents estimated that nearly half of NO-GO decisions acted on invalid evidence. While explicit stopping permissions improved some models, consistent correct decision-making at both GO and NO-GO points remains a challenge. The project code and data are publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32305v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-stage analytical tasks require LLM agents to use intermediate evidence to decide whether to continue, redirect or stop. Self-reflection, in which an agent critiques its output, is widely studied, yet a critique does not show whether evidence changed the next action. We call that capability self-restraint. Existing agent benchmarks largely measure task completion or output quality and leave it untested. DMAIC-Bench evaluates it with 97 seeded tasks across 15 industrial cases in four sectors, built around Lean Six Sigma's explicit statistical prerequisites. Paired counterfactual variants require opposite actions at the same workflow position, distinguishing warranted restraint from indiscriminate stopping. We assess execution traces with a private scorer and final claims through independent expert review. Across 13 models from six providers, execution-level routing accuracy averages 92% on matched GO decisions and 19% on NO-GO decisions, counting any forbidden downstream computation as a route error. Execution traces show agents reporting correct diagnostics before performing analyses that those results disallow. Separately, blinded expert review of the 11 audited agents estimates that reports act on invalid evidence at 47% of reached NO-GO decisions, with an interval from 31% to 61%. Explicit stopping permission helps some models without consistently restoring correct decisions at both GO and NO-GO forks. Sixteen life-sciences tasks in bulk ribonucleic acid sequencing (RNA-seq) and case-control genome-wide association studies (GWAS) show that the same framework can evaluate evidence-dependent decisions beyond industrial workflows. Project code and data are available at: https://github.com/psptpx/DMAIC-Bench-public.

items.title: Researchers release Kolibri, a 78.1B-parameter English-German mixture-of-experts transformer focused on sovereign deployment and regulated domains, with open weights under Apache 2.0 license [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Kolibri: A Sovereign European Model on the Pareto Frontier
items.summary:
Kolibri is a large-scale transformer model designed for specialized use in German and English, particularly targeting regulated sectors like public administration, industry, and aerospace. The model uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 78.1 billion total parameters and activates 3.46 billion parameters per token, trained on 24 trillion tokens including over 20% German data, supplemented by curated and synthetic German datasets. Post-training involved supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on over 1.2 million tasks covering reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval.

The development process for Kolibri was fully controlled, encompassing data collection, architecture design, training infrastructure, and evaluation, ensuring suitability for sovereign and specialized deployment. Kolibri builds on an earlier version called Kolibri Origin and is part of a Model Factory framework that integrates data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows. Among open models evaluated, Kolibri lies on the Pareto frontier balancing quality and serving cost in both English and German.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.31945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This report introduces Kolibri, an English-German mixture-of-experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, released as open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. We built Kolibri for sovereign and specialised deployment, with a particular focus on German and on regulated domains such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. To support these settings, we control the full model-development process, including data, architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, and evaluation. We train Kolibri on 24T tokens across pre-training, mid-training, and long-context extension, with German accounting for more than 20% of the data mix by bytes. To reach this share, we complement German datasets with more than 2T German tokens that we curate from the web with our own pipeline and generate synthetically. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning on curated German and English data with reinforcement learning on more than 1.2M internally curated tasks, which cover reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The model activates 4.4% of its parameters per token, and among the open models evaluated in this report, it lies on the Pareto frontier of quality and serving cost in English and German. Kolibri builds on Kolibri Origin, an earlier iteration that validated our full pipeline at scale. Both models come from our Model Factory, which connects data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows.

items.title: Researchers introduce REACT, an early intervention method to improve safety in chain-of-thought reasoning models by applying conditional activation to initial hidden states [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
items.summary: Researchers present REACT, a technique that intervenes early in chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning by applying a learned safety direction to initial hidden states without altering model weights, aiming to increase safe output generation. The study evaluates intervention timing across the first five CoT tokens on distilled reasoning models, finding the most effective control occurs within a two- to three-token window despite later states being more predictive of risk. On the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B model, REACT increased fully safe CoT-answer outputs from 29.06% to 82.05% on the StrongREJECT-273 dataset while maintaining baseline refusal and usefulness rates.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. But does the point at which risk is easiest to detect also offer the most effective control? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three distilled reasoning models and three generation seeds, the strongest gains concentrate in a two- to three-token early window; on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, the effect falls to approximately zero at the fourth and fifth tokens, even though later states can be more predictive of risk. This separates risk readability from effective control: intervention timing must be evaluated through its effect on subsequent generation. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.

items.title: Researchers introduce Tampered ML benchmark to evaluate large language models' ability to judge machine learning research proposals, finding models perform above chance but remain unreliable [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Tampered ML: Evaluating LLM Judgment of Machine Learning Research
items.summary:
Researchers developed Tampered ML, a benchmark containing 1,858 pairs of machine learning experiment proposals and minimally altered counterfactuals with targeted methodological flaws, to test large language models' ability to identify more methodologically sound research. Human validation estimated 86% of the benchmark items as valid, while leading models like Opus 5 achieved 77.9% accuracy but showed sensitivity to presentation order and a bias toward flawed designs that appear more specific or conventional.

The benchmark aims to support automating parts of AI alignment research by assessing models on hard-to-supervise tasks such as detecting flaws in research proposals and evaluating experimental claims. Despite performing better than chance, current frontier models are far from reliable in this complex judgment task, highlighting challenges in automating research evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One approach to accelerating progress on AI alignment is to automate parts of alignment research itself. Doing so requires systems that can perform reliably on hard-to-supervise research tasks, including identifying flaws in research proposals and evaluating whether a proposed experiment supports its intended claim. To evaluate this capability, we introduce Tampered ML, a benchmark of 1,858 item-pairs, each consisting of an experiment proposal reconstructed from a published machine learning paper and a minimally edited counterfactual that introduces a targeted methodological flaw. Models must identify the more methodologically sound proposal in both presentation orders. A human validation study on a stratified sample estimates that 86% of items are valid (95% CI: 81-91%). Frontier models perform above chance but remain far from reliable (with Opus 5 achieving 77.9% accuracy). They are highly sensitive to the order of presentation and favor flawed designs that appear more specific, transparent, or conventional.

items.title: Researchers find wider head dimensions improve long-context retrieval performance in language models at fixed sizes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Head Dimension Matters in Language Models for Long-Context Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers investigated the impact of head dimension in multi-head attention on long-context retrieval tasks in language models. Their study found that while pretraining loss and short-context task performance were largely unaffected, models with wider heads showed improved retrieval performance and a higher proportion of retrieval heads, indicating more parameters dedicated to retrieval.

The study also revealed that retrieval improvements persisted even when attention module projection weights were frozen during continual pretraining, suggesting that wider heads enhance not only attention updates but also the adaptation of other components like embeddings and MLPs. This highlights the importance of head dimension allocation in optimizing long-context information retrieval in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-head attention retrieves and combines context representations through query--key interactions and value aggregation, with head dimension constraining the per-head representation space. In long-context processing, it remains unclear whether allocating a fixed parameter budget to fewer, wider heads improves information retrieval. In this paper, we investigate how head dimension affects the performance of long-context retrieval tasks. Our empirical studies reveal that pretraining loss and short-context non-retrieval task performance are not affected much by head dimension, while long-context retrieval performance improves with wider heads at fixed model sizes. We find that models with wider heads have a higher proportion of retrieval heads, associating more parameters with retrieval. Our ablation studies also show that the retrieval performance improves with wider heads even when the projection weights in attention modules are frozen during long-context continual pretraining, suggesting that wider heads not only benefit updates in attention modules but lead to more effective adaptation of components such as embeddings and MLPs.

items.title: Researchers propose CoRPS-Dial, a dual-agent framework integrating patient personas and clinical workflows for realistic pre-consultation medical dialogue generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Decoupling Patient Personas and Clinical Workflows: A Dual-Agent Approach to Realistic Medical Dialogue Generation
items.summary: Researchers introduce CoRPS-Dial, a controllable dual-agent system that synthesizes pre-consultation medical dialogues by combining patient personas with guideline-aligned clinical workflow rules. The framework generates dialogues through interactions between a persona-driven patient agent and a process-guided doctor agent, followed by quality control to ensure role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual coherence. Experiments on coronary heart disease data show that CoRPS-Dial improves alignment with real dialogues in terms of information coverage, clinical compliance, and naturalness. Further fine-tuning experiments demonstrate the utility of the synthetic data for medical dialogue tasks, highlighting CoRPS-Dial's effectiveness for clinically grounded and controllable dialogue synthesis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pre-consultation medical dialogues are essential for collecting comprehensive patient information, but are costly to obtain at scale due to privacy and ethical constraints. Existing LLM-based synthesis methods often rely on prompt engineering or rigid rules, limiting their ability to balance clinical relevance with realistic patient diversity. We propose CoRPS-Dial, a controllable dual-agent framework for pre-consultation medical dialogue synthesis that integrates patient personas with guideline-aligned clinical workflow rules. CoRPS-Dial generates dialogues through interactions between a persona-driven patient agent and a process-guided doctor agent, followed by post-hoc quality control for role consistency, workflow completeness, and textual consistency. Experiments on coronary heart disease demonstrate that CoRPS-Dial improves alignment between synthetic and real dialogues in information coverage, clinical compliance, and dialogue naturalness. Downstream fine-tuning experiments further confirm the utility of the generated synthetic data for medical dialogue tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of CoRPS-Dial for clinically grounded and controllable medical dialogue synthesis.

items.title: Researchers use fine-tuned BERT model to predict Austrian National Council members' party affiliations from speeches, analyzing speech similarity among governing and opposition parties from 1996 to 2018 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Analysing Austrian Parliamentary Speeches by Predicting Party Affiliations
items.summary: This paper presents a methodology using a fine-tuned BERT model to assign probability distributions of party affiliations to speeches by Austrian National Council members, aggregating results at speaker and party levels. The study finds that parties governing together exhibit more similar speech characteristics, while opposition parties diverge, and that members who switch parties adapt their speech patterns only after switching. The researchers also publicly release a dataset of party affiliation predictions for speeches spanning 1996 to 2018.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper examines speech characteristics of the Austrian National Council members (CMs). We introduce analysis methodology based on a fine-tuned BERT-Model which assigns to every speech a probability distribution over Austrian parties. These are then aggregated at the speaker and party level. We perform an extensive evaluation to ensure the quality of the generated distributions prior to further analysis. Instead of considering mis-assignments of predicted parties as a performance issue, we leverage them to derive insights about the CMs and political developments. Our findings show that parties that govern together become more similar in their speech characteristics, while, analogously, parties that are in opposition move further away from governing parties. Moreover, CMs who switch party usually adapt their speech characteristics only after the switch occurs. Finally, we publicly release a data set containing party affiliation predictions for the speeches of the Austrian National Council from 1996 to 2018.

items.title: Researchers propose on-policy self-training for large language models using self-generated data and reasoning without external supervision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a self-training framework for large language models that enables self-improvement without relying on external teachers, ground-truth data, or human-curated prompts. The method uses self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations guided only by high-level topic descriptions to synthesize a curriculum for training.

The approach allows models to improve across multiple domains, including text and multimodal tasks like Visual Question Answering, while retaining performance on domains not included in self-training. This demonstrates that foundation models have latent capabilities that can be enhanced without external task supervision or curated problem sets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32770v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy self-distillation enables post-training foundation models without relying on stronger external teachers. However, existing approaches rely on ground-truth question-answer pairs, human-curated problem sets, or other supervised signals. In this work, we reformulate on-policy self-distillation as a self-training framework, driven by self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations. We push supervision to the limit: guided solely by coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model synthesizes its own curriculum of queries and privileged reasoning traces without access to any human-curated prompts or answers. We find that self-distillation on fully synthetic privileged information enables a model to improve across multiple domains while retaining its capabilities on domains it is not self-trained on. We demonstrate the generality of this framework across text and multimodal domains, achieving consistent self-improvement on standard language benchmarks and Visual Question Answering. Our findings demonstrate that foundation models possess rich latent capabilities that can be amplified without external task supervision or curated problem distributions.

items.title: Researchers compare multiplicative and additive state coupling in learned optimizer schedules for MAX-CUT, finding bilinear models generalize better out of distribution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Multiplicative vs. Additive State Coupling in Learned Optimizer Schedules
items.summary: Researchers trained learned optimizer schedules for a continuous penalty relaxation of the MAX-CUT problem by backpropagating through an unrolled classical solver. They found that a state-blind schedule generalizes well to larger instances, while a state-adaptive bilinear schedule outperforms its untrained baseline out of distribution. In contrast, an additive model with similar inputs and outputs performs worse than its own baseline out of distribution, despite being statistically similar in distribution. This performance gap persists without regularization and across weight-decay sweeps, highlighting that the architectural difference in how solver state is incorporated, rather than state adaptivity alone, drives out-of-distribution transfer performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We learn schedules for a continuous penalty relaxation of MAX-CUT by backpropagating through an unrolled classical solver. A state-blind schedule generalizes to instances substantially larger than those used for training. A state-adaptive bilinear schedule also generalizes out of distribution, outperforming its untrained baseline across 15 seeds ($t=4.1$). By contrast, an additive ablation with identical inputs and output heads is statistically indistinguishable from the bilinear model in distribution but performs worse than its own baseline out of distribution ($t=-11.7$). This separation appears without regularization and persists across a $30$ round weight-decay sweep: the bilinear advantage remains significant at every tested value, whereas the additive model never recovers. The results in this setting isolate how solver state enters the schedule, rather than state adaptivity alone, as the architectural distinction associated with out-of-distribution transfer.

items.title: Researchers present TopKLoRA, an interpretable sparse fine-tuning method that enables faithful discovery and ablation of backdoor circuits in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery
items.summary: Researchers introduce TopKLoRA, a sparse LoRA variant that activates only the largest adapter latents per token, designed to improve interpretability in fine-tuning large language models. They demonstrate its effectiveness by fine-tuning models like gemma-2-2b and Qwen2.5 variants on poisoned datasets, identifying and ablating circuits responsible for backdoors without harming instruction-following performance. The method produces circuits significantly smaller than dense LoRA baselines, allowing precise removal of malicious capabilities while maintaining model functionality. The team also proposes a technique using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing to construct model organisms with localized circuits, validating their circuit search algorithm. These findings advance interpretable-by-design architectures that maintain performance and provide faithful units of analysis, with code publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.32866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA.

items.title: Researchers propose AlphaMemo, a self-evolving alpha mining agent using Structured Search-Process Memory to improve factor discovery in financial markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AlphaMemo: Structured Search-Process Memory for Self-Evolving Alpha Mining Agents
items.summary:
Researchers introduce AlphaMemo, an alpha mining agent designed to address challenges in financial factor discovery such as combinatorial search space, noisy feedback, and overfitting. AlphaMemo records reusable evidence of successful and failed edit motifs within specific contexts, using Abstract Syntax Tree differences, confidence-gated residual memory, and veto control to enhance search efficiency and accuracy.

Experiments on CSI 500 and S&P 500 datasets demonstrate AlphaMemo's improved out-of-sample performance and discovery efficiency compared to prior methods. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of its components, including residual learning, confidence gating, AST-diff motifs, and veto memory. The code for AlphaMemo is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.20625v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents are promising for alpha mining via combining financial priors, symbolic reasoning, executable factor generation, and feedback-driven refinement. Yet, they face a combinatorial search space, noisy non-stationary feedback, redundant discoveries, and overfitting risks from naively reusing past successes. To address these challenges, we propose AlphaMemo, a self-evolving alpha mining agent with Structured Search-Process Memory. Rather than memorizing only final factors or full trajectories, AlphaMemo records reusable evidence about which edit motifs work or fail under specific parent-factor contexts. It extracts motifs from Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) differences, applies confidence-gated residual memory on top of a search-ledger prior, and uses asymmetric veto control to suppress high-confidence failure patterns. Experiments on CSI 500 and S&P 500 show improved out-of-sample performance and fixed-budget discovery efficiency, with ablations validating the roles of residual learning, confidence gating, AST-diff motifs, and veto memory. Code is at https://github.com/jarrettyu/sspm.

items.title: Researchers develop TreeWY transform to reduce memory use in speculative decoding of Gated DeltaNet hybrid models, improving throughput and time-to-first-token on Qwen3.5 35B and 397B [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TreeWY: Speculative Verification for Gated DeltaNet Hybrids
items.summary: Researchers propose TreeWY, a tree-structured WY transform for Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrid models that eliminates the need for full recurrent state snapshots during speculative decoding. This approach stores a small pseudo-value matrix instead of per-node states, enabling memory-efficient verification of draft tokens and rollback of rejected ones without architectural changes. Benchmarks on Qwen3.5 35B and 397B models show significant reductions in speculative recurrent-state memory and key-value cache pressure, leading to higher throughput and lower time-to-first-token where memory is constrained, with minimal performance cost otherwise. The method also allows for wider, higher-acceptance draft trees, improving affordability though not yet throughput.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.20961v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern open models are hybrids: most layers are linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet, GDN) layers carrying a small fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value (KV) cache. This makes ordinary decoding memory-efficient, but hurts speculative decoding. To verify a batch of draft tokens and then roll back the rejected ones, today's systems snapshot the full recurrent state at every draft position for GDN layers, and those snapshots cannot be shared across branches of a draft tree, so a wide, high-acceptance tree becomes memory-infeasible. We remove the snapshots. Using a tree-structured WY transform of the gated delta rule, we compute every draft node's output with a single triangular solve and reconstruct only the one accepted state on commit, storing a small pseudo-value matrix instead of per-node states; the derivation depends only on the gated delta rule, not on any other architectural detail. In serving benchmarks on two scales of one hybrid model family (Qwen3.5 35B and 397B) this cuts speculative recurrent-state memory and KV-cache pressure at essentially identical acceptance length, turning the freed HBM into higher throughput and much lower time-to-first-token (TTFT) wherever memory binds, and costing a few percent where it does not. For tree width the same memory buys affordability: a wider, higher-acceptance draft becomes possible, though not yet a throughput win.

items.title: EvoSkill v2 introduces a three-agent system for skill evolution that improves task pass rates by up to 7.7 percentage points over prior methods on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EvoSkill v2: Fully Agentic Skill Evolution from Benchmark Adaptation to a Stateful Evolver
items.summary:
EvoSkill v2 is a three-agent system that evolves the instructions (skills) given to an agent without altering its underlying model. It uses a benchmark adaptor to create task-specific plugins, a solver to attempt tasks, and a stateful evolver agent that rewrites skills based on solver training rollouts at each epoch. This approach differs from previous methods by maintaining state across epochs and accepting all skill updates rather than selecting based on noisy scores.

The system demonstrated improvements of 7.7 and 5.4 percentage points in held-out pass rates over the strongest baselines on SpreadsheetBench v2 and \(\tau^3\)-bench banking benchmarks, respectively. EvoSkill v2 also reduced the cost per percentage point of pass rate gained compared to prior optimizers. Additionally, it enabled a less capable model to improve its own skills, achieving up to a 21.5 percentage point gain in the \(\tau^3\)-bench banking experiment where Claude Haiku 5.5 powered both solver and evolver.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.25931v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: EvoSkill v2 is a three-agent system that edits the instructions (skills) an agent is given, leaving its model and harness intact. The user starts a run by describing a benchmark and supplying a grader, which a benchmark adaptor turns into a benchmark-specific plugin. A solver attempts the tasks, and an evolver reads the solver's training rollouts and rewrites the skills at each epoch. We implement the evolver as one stateful coding agent with a bash tool for the whole run, unlike the two most common designs among the skill optimizers we surveyed: a sequence of single model calls, as in SkillOpt, and an agent that starts afresh each round, as in SkillBoost. We also measure how much the solver's rollouts vary from one attempt to the next, give the evolver several attempts per training task, and accept every epoch's skills instead of selecting among them on noisy scores. With fine-grained ground truth, EvoSkill v2's skills raised the held-out pass rate above the stronger of SkillOpt and SkillBoost by 7.7 percentage points on SpreadsheetBench v2 and by 5.4 on $\tau^3$-bench banking. In both benchmarks and both feedback settings, EvoSkill v2's evolver cost less per percentage point of held-out pass rate gained than either baseline's optimizer. EvoSkill v2 also enables a less capable model to improve its own skills, demonstrated by a gain of up to 21.5 percentage points in the $\tau^3$-bench banking experiment where Claude Haiku 5.5 powers both solver and evolver.

items.title: Scaling Laws for Safety Probes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Scaling Laws for Safety Probes
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30678v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Safety probes trained on a model's activations are a standard tool for monitoring language models in real time. Each time a new model is released or a new harm area needs to be monitored, the probe must be retrained, which requires new labels and a choice of probe architecture. Yet neither the model nor the labels tell us in advance how well the resulting probe will perform. Finding out requires training and comparing many probe configurations. In this paper, we ask whether probe performance can instead be predicted in advance from model size and the number of labels. Existing safety datasets are insufficient for this, as they are either limited in scale or already saturated. We therefore construct six new safety datasets of sufficient size and difficulty. On these datasets, we train two probe architectures on 20 base models from five model families, with 32 to $10^{6}$ labels for each model. We measure performance using probe error, defined as 1 - AUROC, where lower values are better. We find that probe error follows two simple scaling laws. First, the lowest probe error a model can reach falls as a power law in its size. Second, probe error decreases towards its floor as the number of examples increases; the slope increases as the target model size increases. Both laws hold across tasks, model families and probe architectures, and only their fitted constants differ. When fitted on the smallest models of a family, the laws predict the error of the next larger model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases. They also identify whether more labels or a larger model is the cheaper way to reach a target error in 73% of cases. Finally, they choose the probe architecture with an extra error of only 0.006 on average when they pick the worse one. These laws allow safety researchers to determine how to create the best probe for any given model and label budget.

items.title: Dementia-R1: Reinforced Pretraining and Reasoning from Unstructured Clinical Notes for Real-World Dementia Prognosis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dementia-R1: Reinforced Pretraining and Reasoning from Unstructured Clinical Notes for Real-World Dementia Prognosis
items.summary: arXiv:2601.03018v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on clinical text understanding, they struggle with longitudinal prediction tasks such as dementia prognosis, which require reasoning over complex, non-monotonic symptom trajectories across multiple visits. Standard supervised training lacks explicit annotations for symptom evolution, while direct Reinforcement Learning (RL) is hindered by sparse binary rewards. To address this challenge, we introduce Dementia-R1, an RL-based framework for longitudinal dementia prognosis from unstructured clinical notes. Our approach adopts a Cold-Start RL strategy that pre-trains the model to predict verifiable clinical indices extracted from patient histories, enhancing the capability to reason about disease progression before determining the final clinical status. Extensive experiments show that Dementia-R1 achieves the best overall performance on the AMC real-world unstructured cohort, reaching an AUROC of 84.02% and outperforming models up to 10x larger. The framework also generalizes to Parkinson's disease dementia prediction in an independent hospital cohort, achieving an AUROC of 78.37%. On the ADNI benchmark, our 7B model attains the highest AUROC among all LLM baselines at 83.17%, demonstrating strong longitudinal reasoning over fluctuating cognitive trajectories. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/dementiar1-CDB5.

items.title: MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios
items.summary: arXiv:2603.09983v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable scalable performance but face severe memory constraints on edge devices. Existing offloading strategies struggle with I/O bottlenecks due to the dynamic, low-information nature of autoregressive expert activation. In this paper, we propose to repurpose Speculative Decoding (SD) not merely as a compute accelerator, but as an informative lookahead sensor for memory management, supported by our theoretical and empirical analyses. Hence, we introduce MoE-SpAc, an MoE inference framework that integrates a Speculative Utility Estimator to track expert demand, a Heterogeneous Workload Balancer to dynamically partition computation via online integer optimization, and an Asynchronous Execution Engine to unify the prefetching and eviction in the same utility space. Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate that MoE-SpAc achieves a 42% improvement in TPS over the SOTA SD-based baseline, and an average 4.04x speedup over all standard baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/lshAlgorithm/MoE-SpAc .

items.title: Efficient Benchmarking Is Just Feature Selection and Multiple Regression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Efficient Benchmarking Is Just Feature Selection and Multiple Regression
items.summary: arXiv:2605.25773v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficient benchmarking techniques aim to lower the computational cost of evaluating LLMs by predicting full benchmark scores using only a subset of a benchmark's questions. By reframing this problem as an instance of multiple regression with feature selection, we find that existing efficient benchmarking methods can be greatly improved by simply using kernel ridge regression at the prediction stage. Additionally, using an information-theoretic feature-selection algorithm called minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR), we can further improve upon these methods by selecting question subsets that will be maximally useful for prediction. Except in very data-poor settings, these approaches consistently achieve smaller prediction errors (in both MAE and RMSE), and greater ranking correlation between predicted and true scores (in both Spearman $\rho$ and Kendall $\tau$) across a range of benchmarks using both binary and continuous metrics. Furthermore, mRMR subsampling is much faster than competitor methods (which often involve fitting probabilistic models or running clustering algorithms), and is more likely to select the same questions under different random seeds or training data splits. Tutorial code can be found at https://github.com/sambowyer/mrmr_eval .

items.title: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Characterize Then Distill: Mechanistic Reasoning in Large Output Spaces
items.summary: arXiv:2606.06840v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reasoning-trained language models can select, zero-shot, a small set of relevant labels from thousands to hundreds of thousands of candidates. We ask how they do it mechanistically, and whether the mechanism can be distilled. We treat each decision as a token-level event scored by the model's own decision margin: the token that picks a coarse region of the label space, the tokens that pick a label within it, and the token where the output departs from a near-miss named earlier in the reasoning. Attribution, exact mean-ablation, knock-in into another example's context and a null calibration give individual attention heads causal standing. On clinical coding of MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, with all 5,651 candidate codes in context, a small, global, phase-structured set of heads is necessary and sufficient on essentially every summary; distinct head families read the candidate region and the earlier near-miss, and blocking what they read removes their effect; for mentions elicitable in the reasoning, a disjoint mid-layer set makes the region elicitable several tokens before the code. The structure recurs in a second reasoner. We introduce MISTILL, which, unlike chain-of-thought distillation, also supervises the student's pooled attention at these decision events. Read on heads found after training, it nearly doubles the causal recovery of the contrastive decision in a cross-family student and adds a small, seed-stable gain in one that already carries most of it, with no detected task difference at matched precision; under matched selection it exceeds a frozen random-head pool on both recovery and task score. A pre-registered evidence-flip test detected no improvement in evidence-dependent decisions through the tested routes.

items.title: GaP: A Graph-as-Policy Multi-Agent Self-Learning Harness For Variational Automation Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GaP: A Graph-as-Policy Multi-Agent Self-Learning Harness For Variational Automation Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2607.05369v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For robots to work reliably in commercial and industrial applications, recent advances in agentic coding systems have potential to combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model-free policies. We focus on "Variational Automation" (VA), a class of tasks that have larger variations in object geometry and pose than fixed automation. Model-free policies often struggle to close the reliability gap for VA tasks, which must be executed persistently and reliably in commercial and industrial applications. Motivated by prior work on Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and the Robot Operating System (ROS), we introduce Graph-as-Policy (GaP), a multi-agent coding harness that generates directed computation graphs with perception, planning, and control nodes from a Modular Open Robot Skill Library (MORSL). GaP generates an internal simulation environment to rehearse task instances with different graphs in parallel to iteratively refine the graph structure and parameters to improve success rates and throughput. Evaluation with 8 new open VA task benchmarks, 4 in simulation and 4 in real-world, suggests that GaP can achieve success rates that significantly outperform baselines. Details, code, and data: https://graph-robots.github.io/gap

items.title: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20179v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probes on activation vectors are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but their success relies on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons, and recent studies investigated whether this ability extends to language models, reaching conflicting conclusions. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations. We fill this gap with in-context neurofeedback sessions, in which a "subject" model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. In our first experiment, the sentences are generated either by the subject or by a second "writer" model, while the score always derives from the activations of the subject. We test ten open-weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. Is this because the task requires no privileged access, or because the subject controls its activations while processing the sentences, whoever wrote them? To answer this, we prefill a fixed sentence as the subject's reply at every turn and ask it to increase or decrease the score. Three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. We further ask whether models can control their activations to the point of fooling an activation monitor. We make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score. No model learns to lower it, but one model can raise it. In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

items.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy
items.summary: arXiv:2610.30474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) were originally motivated by discovering monosemantic features, a property that characterizes individual features but does not specify what the learned feature set should look like as a whole. As SAEs have increasingly been adopted for attribution, circuit discovery, and intervention, researchers have begun evaluating metrics that describe global properties of the feature set, such as sparsity, dead feature rates, reconstruction fidelity, and disentanglement, a diverse set that extends far beyond monosemanticity. However, this implicit shift beyond monosemanticity has not been formalized as a clear, well-defined objective that comes before these evaluation metrics. Without such an objective, existing metrics remain ad hoc, with their necessity unjustified. In this work, we formalize this ultimate objective by introducing a new paradigm for SAE evaluation: requiring that SAE features, and more generally dictionary-based decompositions of model representations, form an atomic interpretable unit basis, a coordinate system for semantically meaningful explanation. Under this paradigm, we organize existing and new measurements such as DAME (Dominance-Aware Monosemanticity Evaluation) as proxy metrics and introduce a comprehensive benchmarking framework. Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant. These failure modes warrant attention from SAE researchers as targets for improved training and architectures, and motivate dominance-aware evaluation as a standard check for practitioners before SAE features are deployed for attribution, circuit tracing, or intervention.

items.title: Mostly Reading: What Open-Book Scores Measure in Document-Level LoRA Adapters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mostly Reading: What Open-Book Scores Measure in Document-Level LoRA Adapters
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31017v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Single-document LoRA adapters have been proposed as units of knowledge to be merged and retrieved; yet open-book scoring, with the document in the prompt, can credit a document's own adapter (its specialist) for reading that document as readily as for holding it. Training one adapter for each of 150 Wikipedia articles on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we find that open-book scores mostly measure a reading behaviour every adapter shares: a random adapter trained on another document recovers 82 % of the specialist's open-book advantage over the base model but only 2 % of its advantage on a cloze probe that asks for the same document's facts without providing the source text, a share we cannot distinguish from zero. Content does reach the weights, since the specialists beat the base model in cloze recall by 0.094, and the geometry of their updates follows the documents they read; yet, in a test of 30 queries, adapters chosen by weight-space proximity or text embedding are not distinguishable from random ones on either probe, although that test cannot exclude an advantage of about four fifths of what a query's own adapter gains over a random one. At 16 documents or more, correctly scaled merges recover 87 % to 89 % of the specialists' open-book advantage but only 12 % to 16 % of their cloze advantage, with intervals that run from below zero to at most 32 %, against 94 % for joint training. We also report four silent errors, each of which produced a clean, wrong result.

items.title: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Don't Forget What You Just Learned: Self-Directed Repair Turns Agent Mistakes Into Lasting Lessons
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent agents should learn from their mistakes so that experience leads to continuous improvement. Yet today's agents recover from a mistake only temporarily: in-context reflections are easily forgotten across sessions and compete for limited context, while full-parameter fine-tuning is expensive and can interfere with existing capabilities. We introduce Self-Direction, a mechanism for agents to learn from mistakes that combines the benefits of temporary in-context retries and policy updates. When an agent fails a task, it reflects on its own trajectory in order to extract a lesson and immediately distills it into a lightweight low-rank adapter. By keeping the original weights frozen, Self-Direction prevents adapter training from overwriting base-model parameters while training additional parameters equivalent to ~0.02% of the base model's parameter count for each adapter. The agent then saves these adapters in a persistent library of lessons, automatically routing them to solve related problems later. Experiments with agents based on open-weight models from the Qwen family across open-ended research (GAIA), tool-use workflows (Claw-Eval), and terminal tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1) show that our method improves overall success rates by 8.9 to 17.0 percentage points and performs competitively with frontier systems. We find that Self-Direction reduces repeated mistakes across future encounters of a task, nearly doubling the reliability of an agent's corrections. Learned lessons also transfer: a handful of adapters generalize to dozens of new tasks without additional training. Ultimately, this self-directed repair transforms everyday mistakes into lasting lessons.

items.title: Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust--Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust--Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in negotiations on behalf of individuals and organizations, yet they remain vulnerable to manipulation, particularly in repeated multi-party interactions. Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation models, whereas existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon. We investigate whether LLM agents can form useful trust estimates from prior interactions and leverage them to improve future negotiation outcomes. We introduce a repeated, multi-party, multi-issue negotiation framework in which recurring agents participate in a sequence of negotiation games while one participant covertly attempts to prevent agreement. After each game, agents assess their counterparts and maintain pairwise trust estimates that carry over to subsequent negotiations. We compare trust-aware and trust-agnostic agents and analyze how explicit trust influences negotiation outcomes. Our results reveal a \emph{trust--agreement gap}: trust-aware agents can identify the adversary within a few games, but accurate trust estimates do not consistently translate into better agreements. Trust increases agreement rates by up to 23 percentage points, but only when agents are explicitly guided to use it in their decisions. Explicit trust can therefore improve repeated LLM negotiations, but its value depends critically on how trust is assessed and incorporated into agents' reasoning.

items.title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
items.summary: arXiv:2610.31985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings where they pursue separate tasks while sharing resources and operating under review or oversight processes. Such settings create safety risks not only when agents are malicious, but also when they are simply trying to help. Prior work has largely studied adversarial or explicitly collusive behavior; we show that benign agents pursuing separate objectives can spontaneously cooperate in ways that bypass intended workflows. We call this the \emph{helpful agent problem}. We study long-horizon shared-resource environments in which agents sometimes depend on resources owned by their peers and cross-owner changes are normally mediated by a reviewer. When review becomes unavailable, agents begin making changes on one another's behalf despite having no shared reward or explicit incentive to cooperate. Crucially, these actions remain within each agent's local permissions while circumventing the system's intended oversight structure. We introduce \textsc{FavorBench}, a controlled benchmark with measurable downstream side effects, and adapt \textsc{CooperBench} to test the phenomenon in realistic repositories. Across two benchmarks and four models, we find that out-of-workflow favors emerge frequently. Further, in \textsc{FavorBench}, favors from at least three models cause significant harm to parties outside the interaction. These results reveal a distinct multi-agent safety challenge: cooperation itself can create pathways around system-level safeguards.

items.title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.

items.title: Behaviour analysis for large language model-driven agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Behaviour analysis for large language model-driven agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding language-agent behaviour requires learning how actions are organised across a trajectory and how this organisation relates to context and outcomes. We propose a general framework that connects data-driven behavioural discovery with analysis and experimental investigation. Categories developed from recorded activity define what is measured. Analyses preserve the behaviours' positions in the process and express their relationships as interpretable hypotheses. Statistical assessment and tests in held-out contexts examine the strength and scope of the evidence. Experiments, including prompt steering, then test how behaviour and outcomes change under deliberately varied conditions. A study of iterative self-reflection illustrates how discovery, dependency learning and prompt comparisons can inform one another. We develop this approach for trajectories of varying length, event order and agent roles, and identify advances in coding, analysis and experimentation needed to support its wider use.

items.title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low-bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near-optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero-temperature, hard-decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message-Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard-decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2-bit lattice and 3- and 4-bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong hard-decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.

items.title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32177v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

items.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Post-Hoc Rewards: Privileged Reasoning Exploration for Multimodal Embeddings
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have driven substantial progress in multimodal embeddings. Recent methods exploit generative capabilities by augmenting embedded inputs with self-generated reasoning to produce more informative embeddings. However, conventional retrieval supervision for training embedding models specifies pairwise relevance relations without explicitly guiding the reasoning used for input augmentation. Such reasoning is neither directly observed nor uniquely determined by the input, allowing multiple plausible traces to introduce semantic cues of varying retrieval utility. Existing approaches largely optimize reasoning conditioned on the input alone, limiting the exploration of retrieval-relevant traces. We introduce PILOT, a framework that models reasoning as a latent variable and instantiates its prior and posterior distributions as distinct reasoning modes of a shared MLLM. The prior conditions only on the input, whereas the posterior uses additional training-time relational evidence to guide reasoning exploration. To translate the posterior's broader exploration into inference-time improvements, we derive an importance-weighted variational objective and instantiate it as a prior-posterior co-evolution framework that improves both modes under a shared inference-compatible reward while selectively transferring posterior trajectories to the prior according to their utility and prior reachability. On the 78-task MMEB-V2 benchmark, PILOT outperforms the primary baseline across all 12 task groups at both 2B and 7B parameters, improving overall scores by 3.2 and 3.3 points, respectively, with the largest gains in visual-document retrieval (+6.1 and +6.4 points). Our results show that relational supervision is most valuable not as a post-hoc reward but as a signal for shaping how reasoning is explored in training reasoning-enhanced embedding models.

items.title: When Agents Fail: Model or Harness--Who's to Blame? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Agents Fail: Model or Harness--Who's to Blame?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents combine models with execution harnesses, so agentic benchmark performance reflects their joint behavior. We argue that harnesses should therefore be evaluated through their interactions with underlying models. We develop a framework combining five complementary measures: (i) Valid Completion Rate (VCR), how reliably agents finish normally and deliver evaluable results, irrespective of task correctness; (ii) Model-Harness Fit, how well a harness supports task achievement through valid completion for a given model; (iii) Cross-Model Fit, a harness's overall suitability across evaluated models; (iv) Interaction Residuals, pairing-specific execution strengths and weaknesses hidden by component-level summaries; and (v) Token Load, the token demands of agent execution, including failed attempts. We evaluate four general-purpose harnesses (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Pi CLI, and DeepAgents) with four core models, plus two fixed native model-harness systems, on six benchmarks covering context management, tool use, long-context planning, multimodal interaction, and artifact handoff. Including native references and stress conditions, 111 evaluation settings yield 52,168 trajectories. Harness rankings vary across models and benchmarks; task performance and valid completion can favor different pairings, and similar task scores can accompany distinct execution profiles. OpenCode ranks first in cross-model performance, while DeepSeek V4 Flash Preview maintains consistently high Mean VCR across harnesses on the shared four-benchmark panel. These findings support evaluating model-harness interactions, training transferable harness-use capabilities in models, and harness designs adapted to the model and task.

items.title: Do Language Models Trust Their Own Justifications? A Study on Functional Consistency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Do Language Models Trust Their Own Justifications? A Study on Functional Consistency
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely adopted in text classification tasks, where they not only output class predictions but also generate explanations that highlight the tokens deemed most relevant for reaching the predicted label. Yet it remains unclear whether these highlighted elements are behaviorally consistent with the model's own predictions under targeted interventions, which we refer to as functional auto-consistency. While much of the literature evaluates the textual plausibility of such explanations, few studies assess their functional consistency with the model's actual behavior. In this work, we propose an experimental framework based on the principle of auto-consistency: if a model identifies certain tokens as decisive, then isolating, removing, or semantically inverting them should produce systematic and interpretable changes in its predictions. We operationalize this evaluation through sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality metrics, and conduct experiments on IMDB and Steam reviews across both closed-source (GPT-4o-mini) and open-source LLMs (Gemma3, Granite8B, DeepSeek). Results show that GPT-4o-mini follows the expected progression across all metrics, Gemma3 and Granite8B maintain coherence under sufficiency but lose consistency under more demanding interventions, while DeepSeek variants display structural deviations, either failing to preserve sufficiency or overreacting under comprehensiveness and counterfactuality. These findings show that explanation reliability varies across LLM families and scales, with smaller models displaying contradictions and larger ones exhibiting over-sensitivity. By combining sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality, our approach provides a systematic methodology for assessing the functional consistency of LLM self-explanations.
